title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) comparing two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; execution used preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics so each pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We publish artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), present an explicit evidence‑to‑claim table and nearest‑work comparison matrix, and describe preregistered protocol modifications required to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, no transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two contrasting architectural approaches recur in research and practice. Translation‑first architectures constrain the output via vendor‑aware DSLs, apply formal verification, and rely on solver/repair when constraints fail; these prioritize deterministic device guarantees. Agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repairs to achieve correctness while preserving generator flexibility.

This study addressed the preregistered question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation of reachability and safety)—(A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), declared the generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and specified shared_initial_candidate semantics and the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing the two architectures under shared_initial_candidate semantics, with deterministic per‑task validator traces and a complete execution manifest. (2) An explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping that shows which preregistered hypotheses were actually tested under the chosen semantics and which remained unobserved. (3) A compact nearest‑work comparison matrix situating this run relative to representative translation→verify and LLM‑agent NetOps studies. (4) Concrete, artifact‑grounded protocol modifications and operational guidance to convert the present validator‑parity test into a discriminating independent‑generation and repair comparison.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions frame our contribution. First, formal translation→verification work demonstrates constrained translation plus deterministic verification can yield strong device guarantees and support solver‑based synthesis and incremental checks; representative foundational works include network verification and synthesis systems emphasizing soundness and tractable analyses [10,11,12]. Second, LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research examines flexible generation, chain‑of‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair; these studies emphasize deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [3,4,5].

Nearest‑work comparison matrix (compact). The table below summarizes axes that matter for architectural discrimination: independent generation sampling (does each arm draw independent LLM outputs), repair loop instrumentation (are repairs exercised and instrumented), validator acceptance focus (is the evaluation focused on validator acceptance of candidates), and emulator/hardware realism. All entries are grounded in verified artifact records cited in references.

| Work (ref) | Indep. gen. | Repair loops | Validator‑acceptance focus | Emulator/hardware |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| INTA (ICNP 2025) [3] | yes | limited | partial | emulator: yes |
| Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4] | yes | yes | emphasized | Kubernetes policy domain |
| Weighted NetKAT / formal verification literature [5,10–12] | n/a | solver‑based | core | verification models |
| This run (CAND‑2026‑001) | no (shared candidate) | no (repairs not applied) | primary (validator parity) | Mininet‑derived emulation |

The present run differs from prior studies by combining preregistration, archived paired design, and deterministic per‑task validator traces under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the outcome precisely measures validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates but does not exercise independent sampling or repair coverage.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand as the paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B, N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and allowed repair_iterations = 1. The preregistration also recorded shared_initial_candidate semantics and specified paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar test). The preregistration artifact and its identifier are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract. The orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: a single LLM generation per task pair was produced and supplied identically to both arms. Practical consequence: model_calls_used = 120 (one shared call per pair) while planned_episode_count = 240 (two downstream validator episodes per pair). Execution accounting and provider audit are available in execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json. The provider audit confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, demonstrating the execution adhered to contamination controls.

Task generation, validator behavior, and scoring. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task manifest entry contains intent, initial/expected final states, required safe sequences, difficulty metadata, and a canonical reference answer (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative entries). The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: (i) syntactic normalization and command parsing; (ii) required command inclusion; (iii) ordering and dependency checks (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore); (iv) final state consistency (field values on each interface); and (v) a boolean validation_after.valid. A configuration receives a pass only when validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags; these are the canonical evidence used by the analysis executor.

Analysis executor and statistical specifics. Analysis followed paired_binary_analysis_v1 as preregistered. Primary outputs: paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference (A − B), bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) and multiplicity corrections (Benjamini–Hochberg for subgroup tests) were preregistered; secondary analyses execute only when relevant signals appear in scoring artifacts.

Contamination, missingness, and exclusion rules. The preregistered contamination plan enumerated simulator‑to‑hardware fidelity checks (held‑out suite), grammar coverage unit tests for vendor DSLs, and execution isolation measures (fresh model context per call). Tasks flagged by contamination rules would be excluded and documented; in this run no contamination flags were raised (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty) and no pairs were excluded. The missingness plan defined retries for transient API outages and clear rules for pair exclusion; no API failures occurred (execution manifest records failed_episode_count = 0).

sections.discussion:
What was measured — and what was not. The shared_initial_candidate design intentionally removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand. Consequently this execution answers a narrow but operationally useful question: given identical LLM candidates, do downstream translation‑first and agentic orchestration paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) indicates validator acceptance parity for these candidates. The run does not, by design, test whether one architecture would produce more correct initial candidates when operating with independent LLM generations, nor does it exercise repair efficacy because repair_applied = 0.

Operational implications. The experiment is immediately useful for validator regression testing and orchestrator equivalence checks: when validator logic or translation tooling is updated, a shared‑candidate comparator precisely detects changes in acceptance behavior without conflating generator variance. For organizations aiming to compare architecturally distinct orchestrators on independent generation or repair robustness, the preregistered protocol modifications required are explicit and artifact‑testable: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair (model_calls_used would increase to 240 for one initial call per arm); (ii) sample multiple independent generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further increasing model_calls); (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied counters can register nonzero coverage. Each modification will produce observable differences in execution/execution_manifest.json (hosted_model_call_event_count and model_calls_used) and in per‑episode scoring artifacts (nonzero repair_applied fields).

Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_candidate semantics reduce internal variance but narrow the estimand—this was preregistered. Construct validity: deterministic validator rules operationalize correctness but omit operator‑facing properties (explainability, maintainability). External validity: synthetic task corpus and Mininet‑derived emulation limit generality to production hardware; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator limit multi‑model/validator generality. Conclusion validity: perfect concordance leads to a point mass CI and p = 1.0; these are correct statistical summaries for the observed data but do not imply broader equivalence under independent operation.

Reproducibility and recommended follow‑ups. All artifacts cited in this paper (preregistration CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) are archived in the run bundle. To reproduce or extend the study to test independent generator/repair effects, the experimenter should (a) modify preregistration to remove shared_initial_candidate and permit independent sampling per arm, (b) increase model_calls budget to at least 240 for single independent initial draws or higher for multiple samples, and (c) enable and instrument repairs. The run's artifacts provide deterministic seeds and executor parameters (bootstrap_seed = 1729, bootstrap_resamples = 10000) to reproduce analysis exactly.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120; baseline = guarded = 100%), yielding paired difference 0.00 (95% CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false). The run demonstrates how preregistered sharedCandidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity; by design they do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We supply artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a nearest‑work comparison, and concrete preregistered protocol modifications that enable a discriminating independent‑generation and repair comparison in follow‑ups.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
